meta.title: Who really said "Each friend represents a world in us, a world not born until they arrive"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Anaïs Nin — probably. Wikiquote dates it to a March 1937 diary entry, but the popular wording drops the word "possibly," and no page is confirmed.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Each friend represents a world in us, a world not born until they arrive'?
meta.ogDescription: Credited to Anaïs Nin and dated March 1937 — but the viral wording drops a word, and the volume usually cited ends in 1934.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.sourceLine: The line is genuinely and consistently credited to Nin’s Diary, and Wikiquote’s diary-entries section ↗ dates it to March 1937 — but no volume or page has been confirmed against the printed text, and the documented wording reads “a world possibly not born until they arrive.” The popular version quietly drops that word.

source.excerpt: Each friend represents a world in us, a world possibly not born until they arrive, and it is only by this meeting that a new world is born.
trail: Quote Investigator returns “Nothing Found” ↗ for this phrase — the specialists have never traced it, so there is no authoritative ruling to lean on in either direction.
Wikiquote lists it among sourced diary entries ↗, worded with “possibly” and carrying the source note “March 1937.” It names no volume or page.
A March 1937 entry falls within the span of The Diary of Anaïs Nin, Volume Two, 1934–1939, edited by Gunther Stuhlmann ↗ — an inference from the volume’s date range, not a page-level confirmation.

Attempts to confirm the text failed at the source: the Internet Archive’s copy of the 1934–1939 volume ↗ is access-restricted, and the book’s full text is not publicly searchable. That is precisely why the internet keeps citing this one from memory.
source.excerptNote: This is the documented wording, as recorded in Wikiquote’s diary-entries section with the note “March 1937.” Note the word “possibly” — absent from nearly every version circulating online. No fuller surrounding passage could be confirmed, because the volume’s text is not openly searchable.
source.rightsHolder: The Anaïs Nin estate (administered via the Anaïs Nin Foundation) and her publishers (Swallow Press / Harcourt, Brace & World)
source.rightsNote: Not public domain. Every published volume of The Diary of Anaïs Nin appeared from 1966 onward — the volume covering 1934–1939 was issued by Swallow Press and Harcourt, Brace & World ↗ — so whichever volume carries this entry, its first publication is well after 1931 and the text remains in copyright in the US. Nin died in 1977; her legacy is administered by the Anaïs Nin Foundation ↗. The private 1937 manuscript entry itself was never published before 1966, so no earlier public-domain printing exists.

author.name: Anaïs Nin
author.heading: Who was Anaïs Nin?
author.bio: Anaïs Nin (1903–1977) was a French-born American diarist, essayist, novelist and writer of erotica, best known for the journals she kept for more than six decades. Selections were published from 1966 onward as The Diary of Anaïs Nin, edited by Gunther Stuhlmann; her second husband Rupert Pole later served as literary executor and commissioned the unexpurgated editions. Because her Diary is aphoristic by nature — short, quotable, emotionally direct sentences — she has become one of the internet’s most heavily misquoted authors, with lines she never wrote circulating beside lines she genuinely did.

misattribution.heading: What’s wrong with the version you saw
misattribution.intro: The attribution to Nin is very likely right. The quotation is where things slip — both in wording and in the source bolted onto it.

items.why: The documented form reads “a world possibly not born until they arrive.” The version that went viral cuts the adverb. Typical of the trimmed copies ↗: the shortened wording, Nin’s name, and no source cited at all.

The most-copied citation cannot be right if the March 1937 date is. Goodreads files it under Vol. 1 ↗, which closes in 1934 — three years earlier. But neither the date nor the volume has been checked against print, so this is two unverified citations disagreeing, not a proven error.

Sites present this with confident chapter-and-verse. In fact Quote Investigator has never examined it ↗, and the relevant Diary volume is in copyright and not openly searchable — so nobody online is checking the page.

misattribution.truthLine: Best evidence: Wikiquote documents the line with “possibly” and dates it to March 1937 ↗. If that date is right, the Vol. 1 citation everyone copies cannot be — but no one has checked either against the printed page.

context.heading: Why the missing word matters
lead: Nin kept a diary for most of her life, and the published selections are dense with the kind of short, self-contained sentence that survives being cut loose from its page. This is one of them — and like most of her famous lines, it now circulates with no citation attached, which is exactly the condition under which wording drifts.

The documented form hedges: a friend represents “a world possibly not born until they arrive.” The version that spread across social media deletes “possibly” and turns a tentative thought into a confident aphorism. It is a one-word edit that makes the sentence tidier, more quotable, and slightly less like Nin.
detailsBody: A second, more mechanical error travels with the quote. Many of the largest quote pages — Goodreads among them ↗ — file the line under The Diary of Anaïs Nin, Vol. 1: 1931–1934. That volume closes in 1934. An entry dated March 1937 cannot be in it.

By date, the entry would fall in Volume Two: 1934–1939, edited by Gunther Stuhlmann. That is an observation about the volume’s date range, not a page-level confirmation — the book remains in copyright and its full text is not openly searchable, so quotle.info stops short of calling this one verified.
context.pull: One deleted adverb turns a writer’s hesitation into a greeting card.
